questions.q: What is the General Assembly?
questions.correct: NC's state legislature — the lawmaking branch
incorrect: NC's executive branch led by the Governor
NC's highest court for appeals
The council that advises the Lieutenant Governor
questions.why_correct: The General Assembly is North Carolina's bicameral legislature, made up of the Senate and House of Representatives.
why_wrong: The executive branch is led by the Governor, not the General Assembly.
NC's highest court is the Supreme Court, not the General Assembly.
The General Assembly makes laws — it doesn't just advise.
questions.tip: General Assembly = state legislature = lawmaking body.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the General Assembly?
questions.correct: To make state laws and approve the state budget
incorrect: To enforce state laws and run state agencies
To interpret state laws and settle disputes
To appoint the Governor and Lieutenant Governor
questions.why_correct: As the legislative branch, the General Assembly writes laws and controls state spending through the budget.
why_wrong: Enforcing laws and running agencies is the executive branch's job.
Interpreting laws is the judicial branch's job.
The Governor is elected by voters, not appointed by the legislature.
questions.tip: Legislature = lawmaking. What are the two main things any legislature does?

questions.q: Who leads the North Carolina Senate?
questions.correct: The Lieutenant Governor
incorrect: The Governor
The Speaker of the House
The Chief Justice
questions.why_correct: The Lieutenant Governor serves as president of the NC Senate, presiding over its sessions.
why_wrong: The Governor leads the executive branch, not the Senate.
The Speaker of the House leads the House of Representatives, not the Senate.
The Chief Justice leads the state Supreme Court.
questions.tip: Just like the U.S. Vice President presides over the Senate, the Lt. Governor presides over the NC Senate.

questions.q: How can the NC Legislature override the Governor's veto?
questions.correct: A three-fifths vote in both chambers
incorrect: A simple majority vote in just the Senate
A two-thirds vote in both chambers
A unanimous vote from the full General Assembly
questions.why_correct: NC requires a three-fifths (60%) vote in both the Senate and House to override a gubernatorial veto.
why_wrong: A simple majority alone cannot override a veto — a supermajority is required.
Two-thirds is the federal standard; NC uses three-fifths.
A unanimous vote is not required — three-fifths is sufficient.
questions.tip: Override = supermajority. NC uses three-fifths, not two-thirds like the federal government.

questions.q: What is the role of the NC executive branch?
questions.correct: To enforce state laws and manage state government
incorrect: To write and pass new state laws
To decide whether state laws are constitutional
To approve the state budget each fiscal year
questions.why_correct: The Governor heads the executive branch, which implements and enforces the laws made by the legislature.
why_wrong: Writing and passing laws is the legislature's job.
Deciding constitutionality is the courts' job.
Approving the budget is the legislature's job.
questions.tip: Executive = execute (carry out). The Governor's branch puts laws into action.

questions.q: What are the term limits for NC's Governor?
questions.correct: Two consecutive four-year terms
incorrect: No term limits — can serve unlimited terms
One four-year term with no chance of re-election
Three two-year terms
questions.why_correct: The NC Governor serves four-year terms and is limited to two consecutive terms.
why_wrong: NC does impose term limits on the Governor.
The Governor may serve two terms, not just one.
Governor terms are four years each, not two years.
questions.tip: NC Governor: 4-year term, max 2 consecutive. After sitting out, they may run again.

questions.q: How is the NC Governor's term limit different from other states?
questions.correct: Some states have no limits; others allow only one term
incorrect: Every state uses the exact same two-term limit as NC
NC is the only state that limits gubernatorial terms at all
Federal law sets identical term limits for all governors
questions.why_correct: States set their own term limits — some allow unlimited terms, some allow only one term, and some match NC's two-term rule.
why_wrong: States vary widely on term limits — there is no universal standard.
Many states limit governor terms, not just NC.
Federal law does not control state gubernatorial term limits.
questions.tip: Each state sets its own rules. NC's two-consecutive-term limit is one of several approaches.

questions.q: What is the role of the Lieutenant Governor?
questions.correct: Preside over the Senate and take over if the Governor cannot serve
incorrect: Lead the House of Representatives and manage its committees
Serve as the state's chief law enforcement officer
Appoint all state cabinet secretaries and department heads
questions.why_correct: The Lt. Governor presides over the NC Senate and is first in line if the Governor dies, resigns, or is removed.
why_wrong: The Speaker of the House leads the House, not the Lt. Governor.
The Attorney General is the state's chief law enforcement officer.
Cabinet appointments are made by the Governor, not the Lt. Governor.
questions.tip: Lt. Governor = Senate president + Governor backup. Think 'second in command.'

questions.q: Can the Governor and Lieutenant Governor be from different parties?
questions.correct: Yes — they are elected separately in NC
incorrect: No — they must be from the same party by law
No — the Governor picks the Lt. Governor as a running mate
Yes — but only if the General Assembly approves the pairing
questions.why_correct: Unlike the federal government, NC voters elect the Governor and Lt. Governor separately, so they can be from different parties.
why_wrong: There is no law requiring them to share a party affiliation.
NC Lt. Governor is independently elected, not chosen by the Governor.
The General Assembly does not approve the Lt. Governor — voters elect them.
questions.tip: In NC, the Governor and Lt. Governor are on separate ballots. Who might win each race?

questions.q: What duties does the Governor of NC perform?
questions.correct: Sign or veto bills, appoint officials, and command the National Guard
incorrect: Write all state bills and steer them through the legislature
Preside over the NC Senate and break tie votes
Serve as the chief judge of the NC Supreme Court
questions.why_correct: The Governor approves or vetoes legislation, appoints department heads, and serves as commander of the state's military forces.
why_wrong: Writing and moving bills is the legislature's role, not the Governor's.
Presiding over the Senate is the Lt. Governor's job.
The Governor has no judicial role — the Chief Justice leads the Supreme Court.
questions.tip: Governor powers: sign/veto, appoint, command. Which branch do those actions belong to?

questions.q: What are the six roles of the Governor of NC?
questions.correct: Chief executive, legislator, party leader, commander in chief, ceremonial head, crisis manager
incorrect: Judge, prosecutor, treasurer, speaker, diplomat, auditor
Lobbyist, tax collector, police chief, school board director, court clerk, census director
Mayor, senator, lawyer, voter registrar, budget auditor, city planner
questions.why_correct: These six roles describe the many functions of a governor: leading agencies, working with the legislature, leading the party, commanding the Guard, representing the state, and managing emergencies.
why_wrong: Judging, prosecuting, and auditing are separate offices — not gubernatorial roles.
Lobbying and directing schools are not roles of the Governor.
Mayoral and senatorial roles belong to other elected officials.
questions.tip: Governors wear many hats. Which of the six roles most surprised you?

questions.q: What is the role of the Governor as chief executive?
questions.correct: Overseeing state agencies and implementing laws
incorrect: Writing the state budget and submitting it to the courts
Presiding over both chambers of the General Assembly
Deciding which state laws are constitutional
questions.why_correct: As chief executive, the Governor directs state agencies and ensures laws passed by the legislature are carried out.
why_wrong: The Governor proposes a budget but submits it to the legislature, not the courts.
Presiding over the legislature is not an executive role.
Constitutional review belongs to the judiciary.
questions.tip: Chief executive = chief of the executive branch = in charge of running state government.

questions.q: What is the Governor's role as commander in chief?
questions.correct: Leading the NC National Guard during state emergencies
incorrect: Commanding all active-duty U.S. military forces in NC
Directing the state highway patrol and city police departments
Appointing all military officers serving in NC
questions.why_correct: State governors command their state's National Guard — especially during disasters, riots, or other state emergencies.
why_wrong: Active-duty U.S. military is commanded by the President, not a governor.
Police departments fall under local government and the Attorney General.
Military officer appointments are a federal function.
questions.tip: The President commands federal troops. Governors command the National Guard.

questions.q: What are the two types of trial courts in NC?
questions.correct: District Courts and Superior Courts
incorrect: Appeals Court and Supreme Court
Federal Court and State Court
Municipal Court and Circuit Court
questions.why_correct: NC's trial level has District Courts (less serious cases) and Superior Courts (more serious cases, jury trials).
why_wrong: Appeals Court and Supreme Court are appellate courts — they do not hold original trials.
Federal vs. state is a jurisdiction distinction, not NC's trial court structure.
NC uses District and Superior, not Municipal and Circuit.
questions.tip: NC trial courts: District (lower) and Superior (higher). Appellate courts review those decisions.

questions.q: What is the difference between District Courts and Superior Courts in NC?
questions.correct: District Courts handle minor cases; Superior Courts handle major cases with juries
incorrect: District Courts handle appeals; Superior Courts handle original trials
District Courts are federal; Superior Courts are state-level
District Courts use juries; Superior Courts use only judges
questions.why_correct: District Courts hear misdemeanors and small civil cases; Superior Courts hear felonies and large civil cases and use juries.
why_wrong: Appeals are handled by the Court of Appeals and Supreme Court — not District Courts.
Both District and Superior Courts are state courts.
Superior Courts use juries — District Courts generally do not for criminal cases.
questions.tip: District = minor cases, no jury. Superior = serious cases, jury trial.

questions.q: Which types of court have no jury trials?
questions.correct: District Courts and appellate courts
incorrect: Superior Courts and the Supreme Court
All NC courts use jury trials for every case
Only federal courts in NC use juries
questions.why_correct: District Courts decide cases with a judge alone; appellate courts review legal issues — neither uses juries.
why_wrong: Superior Courts do use juries for criminal and major civil cases.
Not all NC courts use juries — many cases are decided by judges alone.
Jury use is determined by case type and court level, not federal vs. state.
questions.tip: Jury trials appear mainly in Superior Court. What decides cases in all other courts?

questions.q: What is the role of the NC Court of Appeals?
questions.correct: Review decisions from trial courts for legal errors
incorrect: Hold the first trial for the most serious felony cases
Set state policy on how all lower courts must operate
Select and discipline all state court judges
questions.why_correct: The Court of Appeals is NC's intermediate appellate court — it reviews trial court decisions to check for mistakes in law.
why_wrong: The Court of Appeals does not hold trials — it reviews decisions already made.
Court policy is set by the Supreme Court and the legislature.
Judge discipline is handled by the Judicial Standards Commission.
questions.tip: Court of Appeals = middle level. It sits between trial courts and the Supreme Court.

questions.q: What are key facts about NC's Supreme Court?
questions.correct: Highest state court, 7 justices, reviews Court of Appeals decisions
incorrect: Lowest state court, 12 judges, handles original criminal trials
Federal court based in Raleigh, appointed by the President
Reviews only local ordinances and county regulations
questions.why_correct: The NC Supreme Court has 7 elected justices and is the final authority on NC state law.
why_wrong: The Supreme Court is the highest, not lowest, and does not conduct trials.
NC's Supreme Court is a state court — justices are elected, not appointed by the President.
The Supreme Court rules on state constitutional and legal questions, not just local ordinances.
questions.tip: Supreme Court = top of the pyramid. How many justices sit on the NC Supreme Court?

questions.q: What is the difference between a statute and an ordinance?
questions.correct: A statute is state law; an ordinance is a local government law
incorrect: A statute is a local rule; an ordinance is a federal regulation
A statute applies only in cities; an ordinance applies statewide
Both terms mean the same thing — just used in different regions
questions.why_correct: Statutes are laws passed by the state legislature; ordinances are laws passed by city or county governments.
why_wrong: Statutes are state-level — not local. Ordinances are local — not federal.
Statutes apply statewide; ordinances apply only in the jurisdiction that passed them.
Statute and ordinance are distinct terms referring to different levels of government.
questions.tip: Statute = state law. Ordinance = local law. Which level of government passes each?

questions.q: What is the role of the Sheriff's Department?
questions.correct: Enforce laws and maintain order in county areas
incorrect: Collect county property taxes and issue business licenses
Manage county schools and set the school calendar
Oversee the county's parks, roads, and public utilities
questions.why_correct: The Sheriff is elected by county voters and leads the county's law enforcement agency.
why_wrong: Tax collection is handled by the county tax office, not the Sheriff.
Schools are managed by the county board of education.
Roads and utilities are managed by other county departments.
questions.tip: Sheriff = top county law enforcement officer. What area does a sheriff cover?

questions.q: What is the purpose of the City Manager in local government?
questions.correct: Manage day-to-day city operations and implement council policies
incorrect: Represent the city in the state legislature
Write and vote on all city ordinances
Serve as the city's chief judge for minor violations
questions.why_correct: In a council-manager government, the City Manager is a professional administrator hired by the council to run city operations.
why_wrong: City representation in the legislature is the role of state representatives.
Writing and voting on ordinances is the city council's role.
Minor violations are handled by district or municipal courts.
questions.tip: Mayor = political leader. City Manager = professional administrator. Which one is elected?

questions.q: What is the purpose of the city council in local government?
questions.correct: Pass local ordinances and set city policy
incorrect: Enforce local laws and arrest ordinance violators
Interpret local ordinances and settle city legal disputes
Appoint the state's senators and representatives
questions.why_correct: The city council is the legislative body of city government — it creates local laws and policy.
why_wrong: Law enforcement is the police department's job.
Interpreting laws is the courts' job.
State senators and representatives are elected by voters — not appointed by the city council.
questions.tip: City council = local legislature. It passes ordinances the same way the state legislature passes statutes.

questions.q: What is an excise tax?
questions.correct: A tax on the sale of specific goods like gas, tobacco, or alcohol
incorrect: A tax on all income earned by residents of the state
A tax on the assessed value of real estate property
A fee charged by cities for licenses and permits
questions.why_correct: Excise taxes are built into the price of specific products — gas tax and tobacco tax are common examples.
why_wrong: A tax on all income is an income tax.
A tax on real estate value is a property tax.
License fees are separate from excise taxes.
questions.tip: Excise = selective. It only applies to certain goods, not everything you buy or earn.

questions.q: How do state governments generate most of their revenue?
questions.correct: Income taxes, sales taxes, and federal grants
incorrect: Property taxes and city license fees only
Printing money and issuing state bonds exclusively
Tolls and parking fines collected statewide
questions.why_correct: States rely mainly on income taxes, sales taxes, and federal aid — these three sources make up the bulk of state budgets.
why_wrong: Property taxes are mainly a local government revenue source.
States cannot print money — only the federal government can.
Tolls and fines are minor revenue sources, not the primary ones.
questions.tip: Think about where your state tax dollars come from. What do you pay taxes on most often?

questions.q: Which branch of NC government does the General Assembly belong to?
questions.correct: Legislative branch
incorrect: Executive branch
Judicial branch
Administrative branch
questions.why_correct: The General Assembly makes state laws — that is the definition of the legislative branch.
why_wrong: The executive branch is led by the Governor and enforces laws.
The judicial branch interprets laws through the courts.
There is no separate 'administrative branch' in NC government.
questions.tip: Legislature = legislative branch. Name the three branches and match each to its function.

questions.q: How many chambers does the NC General Assembly have?
questions.correct: Two — the Senate and the House of Representatives
incorrect: One — the Senate only
Three — the Senate, House, and Council of State
Four — Senate, House, Court of Appeals, and Supreme Court
questions.why_correct: Like the U.S. Congress, NC's legislature is bicameral — two chambers: Senate (50 members) and House (120 members).
why_wrong: The legislature has two chambers, not one.
The Council of State is separate from the legislature.
Courts are part of the judicial branch, not the legislature.
questions.tip: Bi = two. Bicameral = two chambers. What are the names of NC's two chambers?

questions.q: What is the role of various members of the Council of State?
questions.correct: They are elected state executives who lead specific state agencies
incorrect: They are appointed judges who review legislation
They are the 50 elected members of the NC Senate
They are city managers appointed by county commissioners
questions.why_correct: NC's Council of State includes independently elected officials like the Attorney General, Treasurer, and Superintendent of Public Instruction.
why_wrong: Council of State members are not judges — they are executive officers.
Senate members are legislators — separate from the Council of State.
City managers are local officials, not members of the Council of State.
questions.tip: Council of State = NC's team of elected executive leaders, each heading a different agency.

questions.q: Which official serves as NC's chief law enforcement officer?
questions.correct: The Attorney General
incorrect: The Governor
The Lieutenant Governor
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
questions.why_correct: The Attorney General is NC's top law enforcement officer and the head of the state Department of Justice.
why_wrong: The Governor is the chief executive but not the top law enforcement officer.
The Lt. Governor presides over the Senate — not law enforcement.
The Chief Justice is a judicial officer, not a law enforcement officer.
questions.tip: Attorney General = state's top lawyer and law enforcement official.

questions.q: What does the NC Treasurer do?
questions.correct: Manage the state's money and pension fund
incorrect: Collect taxes from NC residents and businesses
Audit state agencies for fraud and waste
Set the state budget and approve all spending
questions.why_correct: The NC Treasurer invests state funds and oversees the retirement system for state employees.
why_wrong: Tax collection is handled by the NC Department of Revenue.
Auditing agencies is the State Auditor's responsibility.
Setting the budget is the legislature's role; the Governor proposes it.
questions.tip: Treasurer = manages money. Which Council of State member handles taxes vs. manages the pension?

questions.q: What is the role of the NC Superintendent of Public Instruction?
questions.correct: Oversee public schools and implement education policy
incorrect: Lead the state community college system
Appoint all public school principals and teachers
Set tuition rates for NC's public universities
questions.why_correct: The elected Superintendent of Public Instruction heads the NC Department of Public Instruction and oversees K-12 education.
why_wrong: Community colleges fall under the NC Community College System, not this office.
Principals and teachers are hired by local school boards, not the state Superintendent.
University tuition is set by the UNC Board of Governors.
questions.tip: Superintendent of Public Instruction = top elected official for K-12 public schools.

questions.q: Which NC court is the highest court of appeals?
questions.correct: The NC Supreme Court
incorrect: The NC Court of Appeals
The NC Superior Court
The U.S. Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals
questions.why_correct: The NC Supreme Court is the final authority on state legal questions — no state court is higher.
why_wrong: The NC Court of Appeals is the intermediate appellate court — one level below the Supreme Court.
Superior Courts are trial courts, not appellate courts.
The Fourth Circuit handles federal appeals — it is not part of NC's state court system.
questions.tip: NC courts from bottom to top: District → Superior → Court of Appeals → Supreme Court.

questions.q: How are NC Supreme Court justices chosen?
questions.correct: They are elected by statewide vote
incorrect: Appointed by the Governor with Senate confirmation
Appointed by the Chief Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court
Chosen by the full General Assembly in a joint session
questions.why_correct: NC Supreme Court justices run in statewide elections — voters choose them directly.
why_wrong: Federal judges are appointed — NC Supreme Court justices are elected.
The U.S. Chief Justice has no role in selecting state court justices.
The General Assembly does not select Supreme Court justices.
questions.tip: State judges in NC are elected. Federal judges are appointed. Which system does NC use?

questions.q: What kind of cases do Superior Courts handle?
questions.correct: Felonies, large civil cases, and jury trials
incorrect: Minor traffic violations and small claims disputes
Appeals from the NC Court of Appeals decisions
Only family law cases like divorce and custody
questions.why_correct: Superior Courts are NC's main trial courts for serious crimes (felonies) and large civil matters, with the right to a jury.
why_wrong: Minor traffic and small claims are handled by District Courts.
Appeals from the Court of Appeals go to the Supreme Court, not Superior Court.
Family law cases go to District Court — not exclusively Superior Court.
questions.tip: Superior = more serious. Felonies + big civil cases + jury = Superior Court.

questions.q: What kind of cases do District Courts handle?
questions.correct: Misdemeanors, traffic violations, and small civil cases
incorrect: Felony trials with jury panels
Appeals from Superior Court decisions
Cases involving NC constitutional questions
questions.why_correct: District Courts are the entry-level state courts handling minor criminal and civil matters decided by a judge.
why_wrong: Felony trials with juries belong in Superior Court.
District Courts do not hear appeals — they conduct original trials.
Constitutional questions are ultimately decided by the Supreme Court.
questions.tip: District = lower level. Think: minor cases, no jury, judge decides.

questions.q: What is the difference between the Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court?
questions.correct: Court of Appeals is intermediate; Supreme Court is the final authority
incorrect: Court of Appeals is higher; Supreme Court handles original trials
They are the same court with two different names
Court of Appeals handles federal cases; Supreme Court handles state cases
questions.why_correct: The Court of Appeals reviews trial court decisions; the Supreme Court reviews Court of Appeals decisions and has the final word on state law.
why_wrong: The Supreme Court is higher — it can overturn Court of Appeals rulings.
They are two distinct courts at different levels.
Both are state courts — neither handles federal cases.
questions.tip: Think of a ladder: Court of Appeals is a step below the Supreme Court.

questions.q: What is a local government ordinance?
questions.correct: A law passed by a city or county government
incorrect: A law passed by the NC General Assembly
A federal rule enforced by state agencies
An executive order issued by the Governor
questions.why_correct: Ordinances are local laws — e.g., zoning rules, noise limits — passed by city councils or county commissions.
why_wrong: Laws from the General Assembly are statutes, not ordinances.
Federal rules are regulations, not local ordinances.
Executive orders come from the Governor — not local government.
questions.tip: Ordinance = local law. Statute = state law. Which level of government is closest to your neighborhood?

questions.q: What services do county governments in NC provide?
questions.correct: Schools, property records, courts, and social services
incorrect: Defense, foreign policy, and interstate commerce
Only law enforcement — nothing else
Managing state universities and community colleges
questions.why_correct: NC counties fund public schools, maintain property records, run local courts, and deliver social service programs.
why_wrong: Defense and foreign policy are federal government functions.
Counties provide many services beyond law enforcement.
Universities are managed at the state level — not by counties.
questions.tip: County government = the level closest to daily life. What services do you use that come from the county?

questions.q: What is a county commission's main role?
questions.correct: Set county policy, approve the county budget, and pass ordinances
incorrect: Enforce county laws and investigate crimes
Interpret county ordinances and settle legal disputes
Select county judges and appoint the sheriff
questions.why_correct: County commissioners are the legislative body for county government — they make policy and control the budget.
why_wrong: Law enforcement is the Sheriff's responsibility.
Interpreting laws is the courts' job.
Sheriffs are elected by voters — not appointed by commissioners.
questions.tip: Commissioners = county lawmakers. Just like a city council, but for the county.

questions.q: What is the primary source of revenue for local governments in NC?
questions.correct: Property taxes
incorrect: Sales taxes
Income taxes
Excise taxes
questions.why_correct: Property taxes on homes and land are the main revenue source for NC counties and municipalities.
why_wrong: Sales taxes go primarily to the state, with counties receiving a share.
Income taxes are collected by the state, not local governments.
Excise taxes are state-level taxes on specific goods.
questions.tip: Local government = property tax. State government = income + sales tax. Who collects each?

questions.q: What is a sales tax?
questions.correct: A percentage added to the price of most goods when purchased
incorrect: A tax on earnings from wages and salary
A tax on the value of land and buildings owned
A one-time fee paid when starting a business
questions.why_correct: A sales tax is charged at the point of purchase — a percentage of the sale price collected by retailers for the government.
why_wrong: A tax on wages is an income tax.
A tax on land and buildings is a property tax.
A startup fee is a business license fee, not a sales tax.
questions.tip: You see a sales tax every time you buy something. It's added to the price at checkout.

questions.q: What is an income tax?
questions.correct: A tax on money earned through wages, salaries, or investments
incorrect: A tax added to the price of goods when purchased
A tax on the value of property you own
A tax on specific goods like gas or tobacco
questions.why_correct: Income taxes are paid to state and federal governments based on how much money a person earns.
why_wrong: A tax on goods at purchase is a sales tax.
A tax on owned property is a property tax.
A tax on specific products is an excise tax.
questions.tip: Income tax = tax on what you earn. Which level of government collects it?

questions.q: What is a property tax?
questions.correct: A tax based on the assessed value of land and buildings owned
incorrect: A tax on wages and investment earnings
A tax collected at the point of sale on purchases
A fee paid when transferring ownership of a vehicle
questions.why_correct: Local governments use property taxes — assessed on real estate value — as their main revenue source.
why_wrong: A tax on wages is an income tax.
A tax collected at point of sale is a sales tax.
Vehicle transfer fees are separate from property taxes.
questions.tip: Property tax = based on what your home or land is worth. Who collects it — local or state?

questions.q: What are federal grants used for in state budgets?
questions.correct: Funding specific state programs like Medicaid, highways, and education
incorrect: Replacing all state tax revenue so states don't need to tax
Paying the salaries of state legislators and judges
Giving cash directly to residents without restrictions
questions.why_correct: Federal grants come with conditions — states use them for designated programs, making them a major budget supplement.
why_wrong: Federal grants supplement — not replace — state revenue.
Legislative and judicial salaries are paid from state funds.
Federal cash assistance goes through specific programs — not general state grants.
questions.tip: Federal grants = federal money with strings attached. States must use them for specified purposes.

questions.q: What does a Governor do as a party leader?
questions.correct: Campaign for party candidates and promote the party's agenda
incorrect: Officially register all voters affiliated with the party
Select the party's nominees for state legislative seats
Fund the party using the state treasury
questions.why_correct: As the state's top elected official, the Governor is the party's most visible leader — boosting candidates and the party platform.
why_wrong: Voter registration is handled by elections officials — not the Governor.
Nominees are chosen in primaries, not by the Governor.
State funds cannot legally be used for partisan party activities.
questions.tip: The Governor is the face of their party in the state. What does a party need from its leader?

questions.q: What does a Governor do as a crisis manager?
questions.correct: Declare states of emergency and direct disaster response
incorrect: Personally lead rescue operations in the field
Ask Congress to pass emergency legislation immediately
Suspend state courts and manage criminal trials
questions.why_correct: Governors declare states of emergency, mobilize the National Guard, and coordinate state agency response to disasters.
why_wrong: The Governor coordinates response — field operations are run by emergency professionals.
Governors work with the state legislature — not Congress — for emergency measures.
Courts operate independently — a Governor cannot suspend them.
questions.tip: Crisis manager = declaring emergencies, mobilizing resources, and coordinating the state response.

questions.q: What is the Governor's ceremonial role?
questions.correct: Represent the state at official events and welcome visiting dignitaries
incorrect: Sign all court orders and judgments into effect
Conduct the oath of office for all state employees
Approve all local ordinances passed by city councils
questions.why_correct: As the state's ceremonial head, the Governor attends ribbon-cuttings, welcomes dignitaries, and represents NC at official events.
why_wrong: Court orders are signed by judges — not the Governor.
Most state employees are sworn in by department heads, not the Governor personally.
Ordinances are local laws — the Governor has no approval role over them.
questions.tip: Ceremonial role = symbolism and representation. Who shows up to open a bridge or welcome a foreign leader?

questions.q: What is the Governor's role as a legislator?
questions.correct: Propose legislation, sign or veto bills passed by the General Assembly
incorrect: Vote on bills as a member of the NC Senate
Debate and draft bills in committee sessions
Appoint members to the House Appropriations Committee
questions.why_correct: While not a member of the legislature, the Governor influences lawmaking by proposing bills and deciding whether to sign or veto them.
why_wrong: The Governor is not a member of the Senate and cannot vote on bills.
Drafting bills in committee is work done by legislators and their staff.
Committee membership is controlled by legislative leaders — not the Governor.
questions.tip: The Governor's legislative tools: propose, sign, veto. Which is most powerful?

questions.q: Scenario: The NC legislature passes a bill the Governor opposes. What can the Governor do?
questions.correct: Veto the bill, sending it back to the legislature
incorrect: Ignore the bill — it never becomes law without a signature
Ask the Supreme Court to block the bill immediately
Hold a public referendum to let voters decide
questions.why_correct: The Governor's primary tool to stop legislation is the veto — the bill goes back and the legislature can override with a three-fifths vote.
why_wrong: In NC, a bill can still become law after a set period without the Governor's signature.
The Supreme Court acts on constitutional challenges, not as a tool of the Governor.
Referendums require legislative action — the Governor cannot unilaterally call one.
questions.tip: Governor + bad bill = veto. Legislature + veto = try to override with three-fifths.

questions.q: Scenario: A hurricane hits NC. Which Governor role is most relevant?
questions.correct: Crisis manager — declare emergency and mobilize the National Guard
incorrect: Party leader — campaign for more funding from party donors
Ceremonial head — attend memorial services for victims
Legislator — immediately sign emergency spending bills
questions.why_correct: When disaster strikes, the Governor's crisis management role is primary — declaring an emergency unlocks resources and authority.
why_wrong: Party fundraising is not relevant during an active disaster.
Attending memorials may happen, but it is not the primary response role.
Emergency bills require the legislature to pass them first.
questions.tip: In a disaster, which Governor power gets activated first — and which law enables it?

questions.q: Which of the following is a state government responsibility — NOT local?
questions.correct: Setting statewide education standards
incorrect: Collecting property taxes from homeowners
Maintaining city streets and sidewalks
Running the local public library
questions.why_correct: Curriculum standards and education policy are set at the state level — local schools implement them.
why_wrong: Property taxes are collected by local government.
City streets are managed by local government.
Public libraries are typically funded and run by local governments.
questions.tip: State sets the rules; local implements them. Who decides what students must learn?

questions.q: Which of the following is a local government responsibility — NOT state?
questions.correct: Collecting property taxes and providing trash pickup
incorrect: Operating the state highway system
Issuing driver's licenses to residents
Setting statewide income tax rates
questions.why_correct: Property taxes and sanitation are classic local government services — closer to daily life than state functions.
why_wrong: State highways are managed by the state DOT.
Driver's licenses are issued by the state DMV.
Income tax rates are set by the state legislature.
questions.tip: Local = everyday services in your neighborhood. State = bigger policy and statewide systems.

questions.q: How does the NC judicial branch check the legislative branch?
questions.correct: Courts can strike down laws that violate the NC Constitution
incorrect: Courts vote on proposed bills before they are signed into law
Judges can veto legislation they disagree with
Courts can tax the legislature for passing unconstitutional laws
questions.why_correct: Judicial review allows courts to declare laws unconstitutional — a key check on legislative power.
why_wrong: Courts do not vote on proposed bills — they review laws after passage.
Only the Governor has a veto — judges do not.
Courts have no taxing power over the legislature.
questions.tip: Judicial review = courts checking the legislature. What gives courts this power?

questions.q: How does the legislative branch check the Governor in NC?
questions.correct: Overriding the Governor's veto with a three-fifths vote
incorrect: Impeaching the Governor by a simple majority vote
Blocking the Governor from commanding the National Guard
Removing the Governor from office without an impeachment trial
questions.why_correct: The legislature's main check on the Governor is the veto override — it requires three-fifths in both chambers.
why_wrong: Impeachment requires a majority in the House and a trial in the Senate — not just a simple majority.
The legislature cannot block the Governor from commanding the National Guard.
Removal requires the full impeachment and trial process.
questions.tip: Veto override = legislature pushing back against the executive. What vote threshold does NC require?

questions.q: How does the Governor check the General Assembly?
questions.correct: By vetoing bills the Governor opposes
incorrect: By dissolving the General Assembly and calling new elections
By voting to break ties in the NC Senate
By appointing the Speaker of the House
questions.why_correct: The Governor's veto is the primary executive check on the legislature — forcing a supermajority to override.
why_wrong: Governors in the U.S. cannot dissolve legislatures — that is a parliamentary power.
The Lt. Governor breaks Senate ties — not the Governor.
The Speaker is elected by House members — not appointed by the Governor.
questions.tip: Executive check = veto. What must the legislature do if they want to override it?

questions.q: Which NC official would you contact about a zoning dispute in your neighborhood?
questions.correct: Your local city or county government
incorrect: The NC Governor directly
The NC General Assembly
The NC Attorney General
questions.why_correct: Zoning is a local government function — city or county planning departments handle land use rules.
why_wrong: The Governor handles statewide executive matters, not neighborhood zoning.
The General Assembly writes state law, not local zoning ordinances.
The Attorney General handles legal enforcement — not local zoning.
questions.tip: Zoning = local. Which level of government makes rules about what can be built where you live?

questions.q: Which NC official would you contact about a change to state income tax law?
questions.correct: Your NC state representative or senator
incorrect: Your city council member
Your county commissioner
The NC Attorney General
questions.why_correct: Tax law is set by the General Assembly — your state representative and senator vote on those bills.
why_wrong: City council members handle local ordinances, not state tax law.
County commissioners handle county government, not state taxes.
The Attorney General enforces law — they don't write or change it.
questions.tip: State laws (including taxes) come from the General Assembly. Who represents you there?

questions.q: A defendant found guilty in Superior Court believes the judge made a legal error. What is the next step?
questions.correct: Appeal to the NC Court of Appeals
incorrect: Immediately appeal to the NC Supreme Court
Request a new trial in District Court
File a complaint with the Governor's office
questions.why_correct: The Court of Appeals is the intermediate step — cases from Superior Court are first appealed there before going to the Supreme Court.
why_wrong: The Supreme Court is the final stop — cases must go through the Court of Appeals first.
District Courts are lower trial courts — a Superior Court verdict does not go back there.
The Governor's office has no role in court appeals.
questions.tip: Court ladder: Superior Court → Court of Appeals → Supreme Court. Which step comes next?

questions.q: Which NC court would handle a shoplifting charge (a misdemeanor)?
questions.correct: District Court
incorrect: Superior Court
Court of Appeals
NC Supreme Court
questions.why_correct: Misdemeanors are minor crimes handled in District Court — the entry-level trial court.
why_wrong: Superior Court handles felonies, not misdemeanors.
The Court of Appeals is an appellate court — it does not conduct original trials.
The Supreme Court is the highest appeals court — not a trial court for shoplifting.
questions.tip: Misdemeanor = minor crime = District Court. Felony = serious crime = Superior Court.

questions.q: Which NC court would handle a first-degree murder case?
questions.correct: Superior Court
incorrect: District Court
Court of Appeals
NC Supreme Court
questions.why_correct: Felonies — including murder — are tried in Superior Court, where a jury of peers can be impaneled.
why_wrong: District Courts handle misdemeanors, not felonies like murder.
The Court of Appeals reviews decisions — it does not conduct trials.
The Supreme Court is the final appellate court — not a trial court for murder.
questions.tip: Serious felony = Superior Court. That's where jury trials happen in NC.

questions.q: What distinguishes an elected Sheriff from a City Police Chief?
questions.correct: Sheriff is elected by county voters; Police Chief is appointed by city officials
incorrect: Sheriff is appointed; Police Chief is elected
Both are elected in separate countywide votes
Both are hired by the county commission
questions.why_correct: The Sheriff is an elected constitutional officer in NC; city police chiefs are appointed by the city manager or mayor.
why_wrong: It's the opposite — Sheriffs are elected, police chiefs are appointed.
Police chiefs are not elected.
County commissioners do not hire the city police chief.
questions.tip: Sheriff = elected. Police Chief = appointed. Which one answers directly to the voters?

questions.q: What is the difference between a mayor-council and a council-manager city government?
questions.correct: Mayor-council: elected mayor runs city; council-manager: hired manager runs city
incorrect: They are the same — the titles are interchangeable
Mayor-council: professional manager runs city; council-manager: mayor runs city
Mayor-council is used by counties; council-manager is used by cities only
questions.why_correct: In a mayor-council form, the elected mayor is the chief executive. In a council-manager form, the council hires a professional manager to run city operations.
why_wrong: They are distinct forms of local government with different power structures.
The descriptions are reversed — the mayor-council has the mayor in charge.
Both forms are used by cities — the distinction is not county vs. city.
questions.tip: Who runs the city day-to-day — an elected politician or a hired professional?

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between state and local government in NC?
questions.correct: Local governments are created by and subordinate to the state
incorrect: Local governments are equal partners with the state
Local governments are independent from the state
Local governments can override state laws with local ordinances
questions.why_correct: Under Dillon's Rule, local governments in NC only have the powers the state grants them.
why_wrong: Local governments are subordinate — not equal — to the state.
Local governments cannot act independently of state authorization.
State law overrides local ordinances — not the other way around.
questions.tip: The state creates local governments. Which level has more power?

questions.q: What is the difference between a city and a county in NC government?
questions.correct: Cities are municipalities; counties are larger subdivisions of the state
incorrect: Cities are larger than counties in NC
Counties govern only rural areas; cities govern everything inside them
They are the same type of government with different names
questions.why_correct: NC is divided into 100 counties; cities (municipalities) are incorporated areas within counties, usually smaller in area.
why_wrong: Counties are typically larger geographic units than cities.
Counties cover all land — including cities within them — for certain services.
Cities and counties are distinct forms of local government with different structures.
questions.tip: Counties cover large areas and handle regional services. Cities handle more local, urban services.

questions.q: What is the role of the NC General Assembly in the state budget process?
questions.correct: Pass the state budget into law
incorrect: Implement and spend the budget once passed
Audit spending after the budget is executed
Propose the budget independently of the Governor
questions.why_correct: The General Assembly votes on and passes the state budget — the Governor proposes it, but the legislature must approve it.
why_wrong: Implementation is the executive branch's job.
Auditing spending is the State Auditor's role.
The Governor proposes the budget; the legislature debates, modifies, and passes it.
questions.tip: Budget process: Governor proposes → General Assembly passes → Governor signs.

questions.q: Which level of government in NC handles public school funding?
questions.correct: Both state and local governments share school funding
incorrect: The federal government funds all NC public schools
Only the state funds public schools — counties have no role
Only counties fund schools — the state has no role
questions.why_correct: NC public schools receive funding from the state (teacher salaries, curriculum) and from counties (building operations and local supplements).
why_wrong: Federal funding exists but is a smaller portion of total school funding.
Counties contribute significantly to school operations and facilities.
The state is the primary funder of teacher salaries and instructional costs.
questions.tip: Schools get money from multiple levels: federal, state, and local. Which level is primary in NC?

questions.q: A citizen disagrees with a new city noise ordinance. Which step should they take first?
questions.correct: Attend a city council meeting and speak during public comment
incorrect: Sue the Governor for signing the ordinance
File a complaint with the NC General Assembly
Ask the County Sheriff to stop enforcing the ordinance
questions.why_correct: City ordinances are made by city councils — attending a council meeting and voicing concerns is the most direct first step.
why_wrong: The Governor does not sign city ordinances.
The General Assembly writes state laws — not city ordinances.
The Sheriff enforces laws — a citizen must change the ordinance through the council.
questions.tip: Ordinance = local law = city council. Who makes it? Who can change it?

questions.q: Which of the following would appear on an NC state ballot — NOT a local ballot?
questions.correct: NC Governor
incorrect: City council member
County commissioner
School board member
questions.why_correct: The Governor is a statewide office elected by all NC voters on the state ballot.
why_wrong: City council members are elected on local city ballots.
County commissioners are elected on county ballots.
School board members are elected on local ballots within a school district.
questions.tip: Statewide election = NC ballot. Which officials appear statewide vs. only in your city or county?

questions.q: What is a state's income tax used to fund?
questions.correct: Education, transportation, health care, and public safety
incorrect: Only the state legislature's salaries
Only federal government programs in the state
Only interest payments on state debt
questions.why_correct: State income tax revenue supports the broad range of state services — schools, roads, Medicaid, and prisons.
why_wrong: Legislature salaries are just a small part of the state budget.
Federal programs are funded by federal taxes — not state income tax.
Debt payments are part of the budget, but not the only use of income tax revenue.
questions.tip: Where does your state tax money go? Think of the big categories of state spending.

questions.q: What type of tax would you pay when filling your gas tank?
questions.correct: Excise tax
incorrect: Income tax
Property tax
Sales tax
questions.why_correct: Gas taxes are excise taxes — levied specifically on motor fuel, built into the price per gallon.
why_wrong: Income taxes are based on earnings, not purchases at the pump.
Property taxes are based on real estate value — not fuel.
A general sales tax applies broadly — the gas tax is a specific excise tax.
questions.tip: Excise tax = specific product tax. Gas, tobacco, and alcohol all have dedicated excise taxes.

questions.q: How does the NC Governor's veto compare to the President's veto?
questions.correct: NC requires three-fifths to override; Congress requires two-thirds
incorrect: NC requires two-thirds to override; Congress requires three-fifths
Both require the same two-thirds supermajority to override
NC's Governor cannot veto bills — only the President has that power
questions.why_correct: The NC override threshold (three-fifths, 60%) is lower than the federal threshold (two-thirds, ~67%), making NC vetoes slightly easier to override.
why_wrong: The thresholds are reversed — NC uses three-fifths, not two-thirds.
The thresholds differ between NC and federal government.
NC's Governor gained veto power in 1997 — it is a real constitutional power.
questions.tip: Federal = two-thirds override. NC state = three-fifths override. Which is harder to override?

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a way citizens can participate in NC state government?
questions.correct: Voting to strike down a state law through a national referendum
incorrect: Voting for state legislators in general elections
Contacting their state representative about a bill
Attending a public hearing on proposed state rules
questions.why_correct: The U.S. does not have a national referendum process — citizens cannot directly vote to strike down laws through that mechanism.
why_wrong: Voting for legislators is the most fundamental form of participation.
Contacting representatives is a core civic right.
Public hearings allow citizens to comment on proposed rules and legislation.
questions.tip: NC citizens influence law through elections, contacts, and hearings — not national referendums.

questions.q: What happens when the NC Governor declares a state of emergency?
questions.correct: Unlocks special powers to mobilize resources and restrict certain activities
incorrect: The General Assembly is automatically dissolved
The federal government takes over all state functions
The Lt. Governor immediately becomes Acting Governor
questions.why_correct: Emergency declarations allow the Governor to activate the National Guard, deploy state resources, and impose temporary restrictions to protect public safety.
why_wrong: Emergency declarations do not dissolve the legislature.
The federal government may assist but does not take over state functions.
The Lt. Governor only steps in if the Governor cannot perform duties — not just during an emergency.
questions.tip: Emergency declaration = unlocking extra executive powers temporarily. The legislature still exists.

questions.q: What does NC's bicameral legislature mean for passing laws?
questions.correct: A bill must pass both the Senate and the House before going to the Governor
incorrect: Bills pass with a majority vote in just one chamber
The Governor votes alongside legislators to approve bills
Bills automatically become law 30 days after introduction
questions.why_correct: Bicameral means two chambers — both must approve identical versions of a bill for it to advance to the Governor.
why_wrong: Both chambers must pass the bill — one chamber alone is insufficient.
The Governor signs or vetoes but does not vote in the legislature.
Bills do not automatically become law — they must pass both chambers and be signed.
questions.tip: Two chambers = double check on legislation. What advantage does requiring both chambers provide?

questions.q: Which level of government would set the speed limit on a city street?
questions.correct: Local government (city)
incorrect: The NC General Assembly
The NC Governor's office
The federal Department of Transportation
questions.why_correct: City governments typically set speed limits on local streets through ordinances — state law sets limits on state roads.
why_wrong: The General Assembly sets speed limits on state highways, not local streets.
The Governor's office does not set local speed limits.
The federal DOT sets standards but does not dictate local city street limits.
questions.tip: Local street = local government control. State highway = state control.

questions.q: What is the difference between an appointed and an elected official?
questions.correct: Appointed officials are chosen by other officials; elected officials are chosen by voters
incorrect: Appointed officials serve longer terms than elected ones
Elected officials always have more power than appointed ones
Appointed officials can never be removed from their positions
questions.why_correct: Elected officials win their positions through public votes; appointed officials are selected by executives, legislators, or other authorities.
why_wrong: Term length varies and is not determined by how someone enters office.
Power level depends on the position — not whether someone was elected or appointed.
Appointed officials can be removed by those who appointed them.
questions.tip: Who picks the official — voters or other officials? That determines elected vs. appointed.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a statute?
questions.correct: NC law requiring all drivers to carry auto insurance
incorrect: Charlotte's rule banning fireworks inside city limits
Wake County's noise curfew for residential neighborhoods
A city's parking restriction on Main Street
questions.why_correct: A statewide insurance requirement is passed by the General Assembly — a statute applies across all of NC.
why_wrong: A city fireworks ban is a local ordinance.
A county noise curfew is a county ordinance.
A parking restriction is a local ordinance.
questions.tip: Statute = state law. If it applies everywhere in NC, it's probably a statute.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an ordinance?
questions.correct: Raleigh's rule requiring residents to sort recycling
incorrect: NC's law setting the minimum driving age at 16
NC's income tax rate for residents
NC's criminal code defining felony offenses
questions.why_correct: A recycling rule passed by Raleigh's city council is a local ordinance — it only applies within Raleigh.
why_wrong: The minimum driving age is set by the state — a statute.
The income tax rate is set by the General Assembly — a statute.
The criminal code is state law — a statute.
questions.tip: Ordinance = local law from city or county. Does it apply everywhere in NC or just in one city?

questions.q: Which NC official manages the state pension fund for government employees?
questions.correct: The NC State Treasurer
incorrect: The NC Governor
The NC State Auditor
The NC Attorney General
questions.why_correct: The State Treasurer manages the NC pension fund (the Teachers' and State Employees' Retirement System).
why_wrong: The Governor does not manage the pension fund directly.
The State Auditor checks spending for waste and fraud — not pension management.
The Attorney General handles legal enforcement — not pension management.
questions.tip: Treasurer = manages state money and retirement savings for government workers.

questions.q: What is the primary way state governments raise revenue compared to local governments?
questions.correct: States rely on income and sales taxes; locals rely on property taxes
incorrect: States rely on property taxes; locals rely on income taxes
Both rely equally on income taxes and property taxes
States rely on federal grants; locals rely on excise taxes
questions.why_correct: NC's state budget is funded mainly by individual income tax and sales tax; counties and cities depend most on property tax.
why_wrong: Property taxes are the domain of local government — not the primary state source.
Local governments in NC do not levy income taxes.
Federal grants supplement state budgets but are not the primary source.
questions.tip: State = income + sales. Local = property. Which taxes do you pay to each level?

questions.q: What role does the NC General Assembly play in impeachment?
questions.correct: The House impeaches and the Senate holds the removal trial
incorrect: The Senate impeaches and the Supreme Court holds the trial
Only the Governor can initiate an impeachment proceeding
Impeachment is handled entirely by the Supreme Court in NC
questions.why_correct: Like the federal process, NC's House of Representatives votes to impeach and the Senate tries the case.
why_wrong: Impeachment power belongs to the House — not the Senate.
The Governor has no role in the impeachment process.
The Supreme Court does not conduct impeachment trials in NC.
questions.tip: Impeachment process: House accuses → Senate tries. That's both federal and NC.

questions.q: Which of the following describes judicial review in NC?
questions.correct: Courts can declare a state law unconstitutional and void
incorrect: The Governor reviews court decisions before they take effect
The General Assembly reviews court rulings each session
Voters can overturn a court ruling in the next election
questions.why_correct: Judicial review is the power of courts to strike down laws that violate the NC or U.S. Constitution — a key check on the legislature.
why_wrong: The Governor has no power to review court decisions.
The General Assembly does not review court rulings — it can write new laws in response.
Voters do not directly overturn court rulings.
questions.tip: Judicial review = courts checking the legislature. Which branch interprets the constitution?

questions.q: What does it mean for the NC Governor to have appointment power?
questions.correct: The Governor selects heads of state agencies and cabinet officials
incorrect: The Governor appoints all NC state legislators
The Governor appoints all NC court judges
The Governor appoints city managers in all NC cities
questions.why_correct: The Governor's appointment power fills executive branch positions — department secretaries and many board and commission members.
why_wrong: State legislators are elected by voters — not appointed by the Governor.
NC judges are elected — not appointed by the Governor (except for mid-term vacancies).
City managers are hired by city councils — not the Governor.
questions.tip: Appointment power = filling executive branch positions. Which positions can the Governor fill?

questions.q: Scenario: A city passes an ordinance that conflicts with a NC state statute. Which prevails?
questions.correct: The state statute — state law overrides local ordinances
incorrect: The local ordinance prevails because it is more specific
Neither prevails — the courts decide which applies case by case
The federal government is called in to resolve the conflict
questions.why_correct: Under state supremacy, local ordinances cannot conflict with state law — state statutes always trump local rules.
why_wrong: Specificity does not give a local ordinance priority over state law.
There is no case-by-case choice — state law automatically supersedes conflicting local law.
A state-local conflict does not require federal intervention.
questions.tip: State > local. Local government only has the powers the state allows. Who wins a conflict?

questions.q: Which official would handle a statewide problem with Medicaid fraud?
questions.correct: The NC Attorney General
incorrect: The NC State Treasurer
The NC Superintendent of Public Instruction
The NC Lieutenant Governor
questions.why_correct: The Attorney General leads the Department of Justice and investigates fraud, consumer protection, and other legal violations statewide.
why_wrong: The Treasurer manages state finances and pensions — not fraud investigations.
The Superintendent oversees K-12 education — not Medicaid.
The Lt. Governor presides over the Senate — not law enforcement.
questions.tip: Fraud investigation = law enforcement = Attorney General's office.

questions.q: What is the difference between the NC Governor's power and the President's power over the military?
questions.correct: Governor commands the National Guard; President commands all U.S. armed forces
incorrect: Governor commands all military in NC; President commands only overseas troops
Both command the same National Guard units in their jurisdiction
The President controls the National Guard; the Governor has no military role
questions.why_correct: Governors command state National Guard units for state emergencies; the President is commander in chief of all federal military forces.
why_wrong: Governors command the National Guard — not all military in the state.
They command different forces — not the same units.
Governors do have a military role — they command the state's National Guard.
questions.tip: State guard = Governor. Federal military = President. Who controls troops during a state disaster?

questions.q: Which statement about NC's 100 counties is correct?
questions.correct: All of NC's land falls within a county
incorrect: Some rural land in NC is not part of any county
Counties only exist in urban areas of NC
NC counties were created by the federal government
questions.why_correct: NC is divided into exactly 100 counties — every square mile of the state belongs to one of them.
why_wrong: There is no unincorporated land outside of counties in NC — all land is in a county.
Counties cover all of NC, including rural areas.
NC counties were created by the state, not the federal government.
questions.tip: NC has 100 counties covering the entire state. No spot in NC is 'county-less.'

questions.q: What is the main difference between how the NC Governor and a City Manager gain their position?
questions.correct: Governor is elected by voters; City Manager is hired by the city council
incorrect: Governor is appointed by the General Assembly; City Manager is elected by residents
Both are elected by voters in their respective jurisdictions
Both are appointed by higher levels of government
questions.why_correct: The Governor wins a statewide election; the City Manager is a professional hired through an employment process by the council.
why_wrong: The Governor is elected — not appointed by the legislature.
City Managers are not elected — they are hired professionals.
Neither is appointed by a higher government — one is elected, one is hired locally.
questions.tip: Governor = political election. City Manager = professional hire. What does that mean for accountability?

questions.q: Which NC official is responsible for K-12 public education policy statewide?
questions.correct: NC Superintendent of Public Instruction
incorrect: NC Governor
NC Lieutenant Governor
NC Attorney General
questions.why_correct: The independently elected Superintendent of Public Instruction oversees NC's Department of Public Instruction and statewide K-12 policy.
why_wrong: The Governor has overall executive authority but the Superintendent has specific education authority.
The Lt. Governor presides over the Senate — not education agencies.
The Attorney General handles legal matters — not education policy.
questions.tip: Education → Superintendent of Public Instruction. Which Council of State member covers schools?

questions.q: What is the NC State Auditor's primary role?
questions.correct: Audit state agencies to ensure money is spent properly
incorrect: Manage the state's investment portfolio and pension fund
Collect state income and sales taxes from residents
Investigate criminal violations of state law
questions.why_correct: The State Auditor is an independently elected official who examines how state agencies spend public money.
why_wrong: Investing and managing the pension fund is the Treasurer's role.
Collecting taxes is the Department of Revenue's role.
Investigating crimes is the Attorney General's role.
questions.tip: Auditor = checks the books. Who makes sure state money isn't wasted?

questions.q: Which of the following requires a jury trial in NC?
questions.correct: A felony case tried in Superior Court
incorrect: A misdemeanor case in District Court
An appeal heard by the Court of Appeals
A small claims dispute in District Court
questions.why_correct: Defendants charged with felonies have the constitutional right to a jury trial, which is held in Superior Court.
why_wrong: Misdemeanors in District Court are typically decided by a judge alone.
Appellate courts review legal records — they do not hold jury trials.
Small claims cases are resolved by a judge without a jury.
questions.tip: Jury trials = serious cases in Superior Court. Not every case gets a jury — which ones do?
